content_voiceover: This slide covers rare blood types, defined as antigen frequency under one in a thousand people, shown here for the Taiwanese population specifically. Two board pearls jump out. First, Kell's K antigen is essentially zero percent in Taiwanese, so anti-K problems are uncommon locally. Second, Duffy Fya is ninety-nine point eight percent positive in Taiwanese, meaning Fya-negative blood is extremely scarce here, the opposite of Western populations, where about a third of Caucasians and the majority of Black individuals are Fya-negative. This population difference drives real transfusion challenges, illustrated by the 1986 case of a French missionary with anti-E, anti-c, and anti-Fya antibodies, where only about one in two thousand Taiwanese donors were compatible, requiring blood to be flown in from France. Key operational strategies for rare blood include rare-donor registries, recruiting foreign donors when needed, frozen red cell stockpiles, and weighing clinical urgency, pre-existing alloantibodies, and hemolytic disease of the newborn risk when deciding how to source compatible units.
